Delirium

tell it from dementia and psychosis, then find the causeDid attention fail over hours to days, and which drug or illness caused it?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Subtypes7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Attention and awareness fail over a short time (usually hours to a few days) fluctuate delirium; dementia starts slowly, attention spared until severe
  • Review every drug first (anticholinergic, opioid, benzodiazepine; meperidine and tramadol highly deliriogenic) stop the culprit treat the cause, reorient, protect sleep
  • Antipsychotic only for severe agitation that threatens safety benzodiazepine only for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
What it is

Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness one more cognitive change

Hyperactive, hypoactive (often missed) or mixed

Driver

A physiological cause: medical illness, medication, substance intoxication or withdrawal, toxin, or several

Proposed mechanism: low acetylcholine excess dopamine

Triggers

Age over 70 non-modifiable dementia (a leading risk factor) or mild cognitive impairment

Drugs (up to 39% of cases) surgery, hypoxia, untreated pain, infection

Male sex non-modifiable functional disabilities, poor vision and hearing, frailty

Chain

Vulnerable patient precipitant (drug, surgery, infection) inattention over hours to days

Fluctuates through the day, often worse at night

Usually reversible, though deficits often take weeks or months to clear

Insights

Sleepy and quiet with an acute change test attention; inattention points to hypoactive delirium, often mistaken for depression

New psychosis in an older adult: usually delirium or dementia; a primary psychosis rarely starts in old age

Dementia and complications, in detaildetail behind the chain
With dementiaAn estimated 20% to 50% of hospitalized patients with dementia may develop deliriumask someone who knows the patient for the baseline
ComplicationsFalls and injuries, aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers, dehydration and electrolyte disorders
2Urgent risks
WithdrawalDelirium tremens: confusion, fleeting hallucinations, tremor, sweating, fever and a fast pulse, usually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink
It can be fatal: treat it promptly

If alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal is the cause, choose an intravenous (IV) benzodiazepine; in alcohol withdrawal, no haloperidol at first.

DangerAgitation that puts the patient or others at risk
Restraint only to prevent harm

If it threatens safety despite nonpharmacologic care and withdrawal is excluded, choose a low-dose antipsychotic, with a baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) for the QTc (rate-corrected QT interval), especially with haloperidol.

NeurologicNew focal sign or head trauma

If a subdural bleed or stroke is possible, choose noncontrast CT (computed tomography) of the head, the first-line scan.

InfectionSuspected bacterial meningitis

If lumbar puncture must wait for imaging, choose blood cultures, then antibiotics and a glucocorticoid before the scan.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
DeliriumInattention, disorientation, visual hallucinations or delusionsHours to a few days, fluctuating through the day; evidence of a medical, drug or withdrawal cause
Paranoid delusions; hallucinations mainly auditoryAttention and orientation intact; no medical cause; usually slow onset with a prodrome, often in adolescence or young adulthood, rarely in old age
Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)Memory lost, especially recent events; stable day to daySlow, uncertain start; attention spared until severe
Depressed mood or lost interest, 5 or more symptoms; attention and consciousness preserved2 weeks or more; an acute change with inattention is hypoactive delirium instead
Dementia with Lewy bodiesFluctuating cognition, visual hallucinationsSwings usually span days to weeks, within a chronic dementia
Delirium on top of dementiaKnown dementia, new drowsiness or agitationAn acute change from the baseline given by someone who knows the patient
Sweating, tremor, fever, fast pulse, fleeting hallucinationsUsually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink; treated with a benzodiazepine
Tremor and agitationIn the NBME case, thyroxine treated her hypothyroidism and was not counted as the cause
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Meperidine with a high creatinineNormeperidine accumulatingStop it; treat the pain another way
A new first-generation antihistamine for sleepA highly anticholinergic drugStop it
Focal weakness after a fall on an anticoagulantSubdural hemorrhageNoncontrast head CT: head trauma is itself an indication; a focal sign best predicts an abnormal scan
Confusion, tremor, sweating, fast pulse 48 to 72 hours after the last drinkDelirium tremensIV benzodiazepine
Takes a benzodiazepine; confused, tremulous, tachycardic after stoppingBenzodiazepine withdrawal: short-acting within 1 to 2 days, long-acting several days to a weekIV benzodiazepine, the drug of choice for withdrawal delirium

Pause point. The bait: new paranoid delusions offered as a primary psychosis, or a tremor offered as too much thyroxine. Disorientation to time with delusions days after surgery points to delirium; confirm inattention and fluctuation, then read the drug list for the opioid (meperidine), anticholinergic or benzodiazepine.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: delirium Attention – attention and awareness disturbed · Onset – over a short time (usually hours to a few days), a change from baseline, tending to fluctuate during the day · Cognition – one more disturbance: memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception · Exclusion – not better explained by a preexisting, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder, and not in severely reduced arousal such as coma · Cause – evidence of a medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, toxin, or several · Against dementia and psychosis – timing chart
Bedside screenA bedside screen: acute onset with a fluctuating course and inattention are both required, plus either disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness.
6Subtypes
Delirium subtypes
SubtypeRecognize itIt means
HyperactiveAgitated, more sympathetic activity; occasionally combativeAntipsychotic only if safety is threatened
HypoactiveSomnolent, low arousal, sluggishOften missed or called depression; test attention
MixedSwings between the twoTest attention in either phase
7Treatment
1

Every patientfrom the start

Treat the cause; stop deliriogenic drugs; reorient; glasses and hearing aids; protect sleep; mobilize

Nonpharmacologic care is the main treatment.

2

Severe agitationbehavior puts the patient or others at risk and withdrawal is excluded

Low-dose antipsychotic: haloperidol, quetiapine or risperidone

Baseline ECG for the QTc, especially with haloperidol; adjust the dose daily and stop it as soon as clinically feasible. It is not shown to shorten delirium.

Restraint: at any rung, only to prevent harm; trained staff apply it, release it at least every 2 hours and stop it as soon as possible

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawalIV benzodiazepine, the drug of choiceNo haloperidol at first in alcohol withdrawal: it may lower the seizure threshold
Any other causeTreat the cause; no benzodiazepine for the delirium itselfBenzodiazepines bring more confusion and sedation
Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia, with severe agitationQuetiapine, pimavanserin or clozapineRisperidone, olanzapine and typical antipsychotics aggravate parkinsonism; in Lewy body dementia even very low doses may acutely worsen it
Meperidine or another deliriogenic opioidStop it; treat the pain another wayNormeperidine builds up when the kidneys clear it poorly
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
At-risk patient, before deliriumIdentify the risk; fewer disturbances, protect sleep, frequent reorientation, mobility; no antipsychotic to prevent it Guideline detailAvoid meperidine in older adults (its neurotoxicity, delirium included, may exceed other opioids’). With delirium or a high risk of it, also avoid anticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids, histamine-2 receptor antagonists, zolpidem-type hypnotics and opioids, except in listed situations.
Talking with the familyTell them it is usually reversible, but deficits often take weeks or months to clear
After dischargeCounsel: decline, institutionalization and death stay more likely for up to 2 years
Practice
  1. 72-year-old man 2 days after hip replacement since last night sees children in his room says staff stole his wallet calm mornings, agitated evenings No psychiatric history vital signs normal · fails days of the week backward · oriented to person only → Delirium → acute, fluctuating inattention with visual hallucinations and disorientation after surgery is delirium
  2. 78-year-old woman, 2 years of worsening forgetfulness repeats questions; misses bills lost driving a familiar route no day-to-day fluctuation alert · days backward correct · 0 of 3 words recalled · disoriented to date only · afebrile; vitals, blood count, chemistry, thyroid normal → Major neurocognitive disorder → slow onset over years, memory lost first, attention spared: dementia, not delirium
  3. 84-year-old woman, pneumonia, hospital day 3 drowsy; one-word answers cannot count backward from 20 son: sharp last week; is she depressed? No history of depression oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L/min · other vital signs normal · oriented to person only → Hypoactive delirium → somnolent and inattentive with an acute change from last week: hypoactive delirium, often mistaken for depression
  4. 81-year-old woman in the hospital for cellulitis given diphenhydramine for sleep last evening, her first dose overnight: confused, picks at the air T 37.4 °C · HR 104/min · BP 136/80 · inattentive · oriented to person only → Anticholinergic effect → first-generation antihistamines are highly anticholinergic, a Beers delirium class
  5. 86-year-old woman from a nursing home with 1 day of confusion that comes and goes at baseline oriented; walks with a cane no new medications Neurologic examination nonfocal T 37.8 °C · HR 98/min · BP 124/70 · inattentive · oriented to person only → CBC, metabolic panel and urinalysis → look for the medical cause first; imaging is not routine without focal signs
  6. 77-year-old man taking warfarin fell at home 2 days ago now drowsy and confused, worse at night new weakness of the right arm Blood count and chemistry normal T 36.9 °C · HR 84/min · BP 164/90 · inattentive · oriented to person only → CT of the head without contrast → a focal sign after head trauma on an anticoagulant: look for a subdural hemorrhage
  7. 69-year-old man 2 days after knee replacement restless; says someone hides in the closet fluctuating meperidine every 4 hours for pain Not dangerous to himself or others vital signs normal · creatinine 2.1 mg/dL · inattentive · oriented to person and place → Replace meperidine with another analgesic → stop the deliriogenic drug; poor kidney clearance lets normeperidine accumulate; untreated pain also precipitates delirium, so give another analgesic
  8. 80-year-old man after bowel surgery yesterday pulls his IV, climbs bed rails, hits a nurse despite reorientation, daughter present Infection, pain treated; sedatives stopped; no alcohol T 37.6 °C · HR 102/min · BP 150/88 · inattentive · oriented to person only · QTc normal → Low-dose haloperidol → severe agitation that threatens safety despite nonpharmacologic care: low-dose antipsychotic after a QTc check
  9. 52-year-old man admitted 2 days ago for femur fracture now confused, sweaty and tremulous picks at insects he sees on sheets drank 10 beers a day until admission T 38.3 °C · HR 128/min · BP 168/98 · inattentive · oriented to person only → Intravenous benzodiazepine → alcohol withdrawal delirium, usually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink: benzodiazepines are the drug of choice
  10. 83-year-old woman on day 2 of ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection restless and calling out at night; calmer by day not harming herself or others No alcohol or sedative use vital signs normal · inattentive · oriented to person and place → Lorazepam at bedtime → benzodiazepines worsen confusion and sedation outside withdrawal; keep treating the infection
  11. 79-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment admitted for an elective hip replacement tomorrow wears glasses and hearing aids Alert and attentive oriented to person, place and time · vital signs normal → Reorientation, mobilization and sleep protection → targeted nonpharmacologic prevention; antipsychotics are not shown to prevent episodes, and zolpidem is on the Beers delirium list
  12. 81-year-old woman, Alzheimer disease for 3 years baseline: knows family, dresses herself 1 day of drowsiness alternating with shouting cannot follow a conversation; dysuria T 38.4 °C · HR 104/min · BP 118/70 · inattentive · oriented to person only · urine: leukocyte esterase, nitrites → Delirium from a urinary tract infection → an acute change from her baseline with fever and dysuria is delirium, and dementia is a leading risk factor; Lewy body fluctuations usually span days to weeks within a chronic dementia and do not explain fever or dysuria
  13. 68-year-old woman admitted 2 days ago for pyelonephritis nightly alprazolam for years; not ordered here since last night: sleepless, tremulous, hallucinating Antibiotic covers the cultured organism T 37.0 °C · BP 166/94 mm Hg · HR 110/min · oriented to name only → Benzodiazepine withdrawal → a long-term benzodiazepine stopped on admission; withdrawal follows within days, depending on half-life, can be life-threatening and is treated by restarting a benzodiazepine; she is afebrile on an antibiotic that covers the organism
How NBME framed it: question 1

57-year-old woman; tibial fracture fixed (open reduction, internal fixation) 4 days ago now agitated; believes the nurses are experimenting on her and keep her from sleeping says the nurses are trying to poison her appears tremulous Hypertension, systemic lupus erythematosus; no psychiatric illness or substance abuse Medications: chloroquine, hydrochlorothiazide, meperidine, propranolol, thyroxine oriented to person and place, not time

Which drug most likely caused her symptoms?

Competing answers
  • Chloroquine: a daily drug she takes for lupus; but the explanation clears all four non-opioid options: none is linked to delirium or on the Beers list.
  • Hydrochlorothiazide: her antihypertensive; but not linked to delirium in the explanation.
  • Propranolol: a beta blocker that also treats tremor, and she is tremulous; but not linked to delirium in the explanation.
  • Thyroxine: tremor and agitation suggest too much thyroid hormone; but it treats hypothyroidism and is not linked to delirium in the explanation.

Down to two: meperidine or thyroxine. Meperidine: new agitation, disorientation to time and paranoid delusions days after surgery is delirium, and she takes an opioid. The explanation names anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines as common causes and calls meperidine and tramadol highly deliriogenic; no psychiatric or substance history argues against a primary psychosis or withdrawal. Thyroxine treats hypothyroidism and is not linked to delirium in the explanation.

Pairs with Psychosis: exclude a medical cause first; acute onset over hours to days suggests one.
Transferable rule

In a new psychosis or confusion in a hospitalized or older patient, test attention and ask when it began: acute, fluctuating inattention points to delirium. Then read the medication list and stop the anticholinergic, opioid or benzodiazepine that started it.
